analysis.one_liner: Bars credit card issuers from cutting off cardholders or discriminating based on where they live.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote; it sat in a House Banking subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop credit card companies from canceling a card and demanding the whole balance at once, and from cutting credit limits below what a person already owes. It would bar companies from judging applicants by their zip code or region — a practice that can quietly screen out people from poorer or minority neighborhoods. It would also require 60 days' notice before a company changes card terms and ban arbitrary changes, with exceptions for fraud, default, or a real change in the borrower's finances.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card holders, especially people who live in neighborhoods or regions that lenders use as a shorthand for risk. The bill would stop the practice of cutting a card's limit below an existing balance and demanding immediate repayment of the difference — a move that can force someone with a balance into sudden debt trouble. It would also give all cardholders 60 days' notice before their terms change and forbid arbitrary changes to interest or fees.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a card issuer from unilaterally closing an account and demanding immediate repayment of the outstanding balance, and from cutting the credit limit below the existing balance and demanding immediate repayment of the excess; exceptions apply to fraud and to failure to meet repayment terms [S2][S3].

Adds geographic region and residence location — including zip code or census tract used to judge neighborhood demographics — to the prohibited grounds for discrimination under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, and bars card issuers from taking any adverse action on that basis under the Truth in Lending Act [S2][S3].

Bars card agreements from allowing unilateral changes to key terms before a 60-day notice period ends, prohibits arbitrary or capricious changes, and requires the Federal Reserve to write rules governing credit scoring systems and to study how accurately those systems predict risk [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers and banks would bear the cost: they could no longer cut off borrowers or demand accelerated repayment as a risk-management tool, could not price or screen by region or neighborhood, and would face new limits on changing account terms. Cardholders with genuinely worsening finances would still face reduced credit under the exceptions, but lenders' general flexibility would shrink.

drawbacks.text: Lenders use account closures, limit cuts, and geographic screening to manage risk; restricting these tools could make some card issuers less willing to extend credit at all, or push them to charge everyone higher rates to cover borrowers they can no longer cut off individually [S2][S3].

The bill itself acknowledges the tension: it directs the Federal Reserve to design a credit risk model that both protects institutions from excessive risk and keeps credit available, an acknowledgment that the new rules could squeeze credit availability if done wrong [S2][S3].

Some geographic screening may reflect real differences in default risk rather than prejudice, and blanket bans on using location data would remove a tool lenders argue keeps pricing honest for everyone else.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For cardholders carrying balances, the protections are concrete: no sudden demand for the whole balance, notice before terms change, and no neighborhood-based discrimination. The honest cost is that lenders losing these risk tools might restrict who gets cards or raise rates for everyone; the bill's own carve-outs for default and genuine financial change show it tried to preserve lenders' core protections, so the design is narrower than a total ban on risk management.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the House Banking Committee, passed to its consumer affairs subcommittee, and died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph P. Kennedy II introduced the bill on March 22, 1991, with Rep. Edward Markey as its sole cosponsor [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs, which in turn referred it to the Subcommittee on Consumer Affairs and Coinage on April 1, 1991 [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no markup, no floor vote, no Senate companion — the bill died in subcommittee when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers came out ahead: the bill died in subcommittee, so they kept the ability to close accounts, demand accelerated repayment, cut limits, change terms unilaterally, and screen applicants by neighborhood. Cardholders got none of the protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit card issuers, which kept full discretion

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only two supporters in the record, Kennedy and Markey, were both Massachusetts Democrats; no Republican support appears anywhere in the record, and no vote ever occurred.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
industries.note: The bill would strip issuers of several tools: unilateral account closures and balance acceleration, cuts below existing balances, unilateral term changes without 60 days' notice, and neighborhood- or region-based screening. Those tools are used to manage risk, but the geographic-screening ban targets a practice that can quietly exclude people based on where they live, which is why the bill treats the industry's interest as running against cardholders'.

The bill would subject credit review scoring systems to Federal Reserve methodology rules while also commissioning a federal study and model that could legitimize scoring when done fairly. Scoring firms would face new constraints but also a government-backed framework for their use.
